title: Medical ethics: principles, consent and the Hippocratic tradition
note: Clinical ethics is often organized around four principles: respect for autonomy, beneficence, non-maleficence and justice. Informed consent puts autonomy into practice. Research ethics grew from hard lessons, recorded in the Nuremberg Code, the Declaration of Helsinki and the Belmont Report.

read.title: What informed consent requires
text: Informed consent is not a signature; it is a process. It rests on respect for autonomy, the idea that capable adults have the right to decide what is done to their own bodies. A signed form only records that the process happened.

Several elements must be present. The patient needs decision-making capacity: the ability to understand the relevant information, appreciate how it applies to their situation, reason about the options and communicate a choice. The clinician must disclose the nature of the proposed treatment, its expected benefits, its significant risks, the reasonable alternatives, and what would likely happen with no treatment. The patient must actually understand that information, so it has to be explained in plain language and checked. Finally, the choice must be voluntary, free of coercion or undue pressure.

Capacity is specific to a decision and can change, so a person may be able to make a simple choice but not a complex one. When a patient lacks capacity, a surrogate decides, ideally using substituted judgment, choosing as the patient would have chosen. In a true emergency, when an unconscious patient needs urgent treatment and no one can consent, clinicians may act to prevent serious harm.
